content.en: It's late 2016. We are on the opening panel of the North India Regional Conference of the IAWS on, 'Documenting Women's Experiences in the Movement: Issues, Experiences and Struggles' in Ranchi. A number of questions confront us. How to present an overview of more than thirty-five years of an activist group? Which accounts can best illustrate the twists and turns of our many campaigns, many journeys? What reflections can generate useful discussions on what's been gained and lost over the decades? What contemplations on our organisational structure and functioning should we focus on? What narratives can make meaningful contribution to contemporary debates and questions of women's movements in India that we have gathered here to discuss today? Asked to focus on our work related to women's health, we frame those campaigns within the rubric of violence against women by corporations and the State. Reflecting on how those strategies find resonance in other campaigns targeted against the State as well as communal, sectarian, misogynist, homophobic forces in society, we bring within the ambit of the discussion, our commitment to generating vibrant debates with friends and comrades in our shared struggles. Because like most feminists we believe that change starts from within.

But first, a brief backgrounder - Saheli started in New Delhi in 1981 primarily as a crisis intervention centre. Like many of the earliest autonomous groups in the country, our struggles against oppression and violence within marriage, family and community led to vibrant campaigns against dowry, domestic violence, rape, sexual harassment, communalism, war, and discrimination against women in the law. Our work on women's health involved long standing campaigns against coercive population control policies, hazardous contraceptives, sex-determination, the unethical sale of emergency    contraceptives, and vaccines against cervical cancer. Not surprisingly, the challenges have been many and complex, and so have been our strategies to confront them.

Since the late 1970s, when women's groups began to publicly challenge violence against women it was the first step to breaking the silence surrounding it, visibilising it and taking it out of the 'private' domain to make it a public concern. Thus, while challenging the violence of one citizen against another, we exposed the structures that sustain (and even legitimise) such violence: the power of patriarchy, the inequities of gender, the oppression of women within institutions of marriage, family and community, and of course, most critically, the State and its institutions. Be it in the cases of dowry related murders such as that of Sudha Goel, or Kanchanbala, the daughter of that fiery activist, Satyarani Chaddha; the 'Sati' murder of Roop Kanwar of Deorala or even, decades later, that of Charanshah of Mahoba. But well before these legendary battles of the autonomous women's movements came to be, by the turn of 1980, a series of instances of custodial violence - the rape of a young Adivasi woman in Maharashtra, Mathura (and the subsequent acquittal of the guilty by the Supreme Court); the sexual assault and parading of Maya Tyagi in Baghpat District, and Rameeza Bee in Hyderabad, among others - catalysed the coming together of many feminist groups across the country as autonomous women's 'movements', as we prefer to call ourselves today.

So, what does it mean for Saheli to be autonomous? When Saheli came into being, it was a time when women from many Left parties, socialist formations and people's movements were seeking political spaces that would be more responsive to women and women's issues. We were talking about what affected us as women — in such a context, our organisational autonomy from both, political parties and the State, was and remains, central.

Likewise on funding, we maintain our distance from institutional agendas and support, both Indian and international. While members have 'other' jobs/ occupations to earn their living, we sustain our organisational work through individual donations, periodic fund raising efforts and contributions gathered against publications. This autonomy is reflected in our choice of work and strategy, as much as it informs our effort to work outside the framework of hierarchical structures, as a feminist collective, with all its strengths and limitations.

One of the important legacies of feminist activism is the refusal to be intimidated by the power of any 'specialised' knowledge, be it legal, medical or economic. As our work as a crisis intervention centre helped us uncover the gender biases in laws and cultural practices across communities, we engaged with religious personal laws, customary practices, secular laws, and the gender biases of the legal and judicial machinery. Every intervention in the arena of law/legal reform - be it sexual assault, representation of women in the media, domestic violence, Section 377 of the IPC, communal violence, changes in Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC), the Sexual Assault Bill or in fact even the Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (PCPNDT) Act that emerged after a nationwide campaign against sex selective abortions - has required us to develop specific areas of knowledge and expertise within the group as the foundation on which we build a collective understanding and take a position on the matter.

Over time, our understanding of violence on women became more expansive, recognising women's health as a political site of violence by the State. Consider this - the period of the Emergency from 1975-1977 is recognised for widespread violence and repression by the State which included, among its horrors, the forced sterilisations of men in camps. Ever since the period of the Emergency, the focus of the State's family planning policies and programmes has shifted entirely to the women of this country whose health and wellbeing has been systematically jeopardised by the State, its institutions and policies through coercive population control, forced, unsafe and early sterilisations, and unethical trials on poor, Dalit and Adivasi women and girls of hazardous long-acting, hormonal contraceptives like Net-En, Norplant and Depo Provera, chemical sterilisation methods such as Quinacrine, vaccines against cervical cancer. Countless actions of the State that fall firmly within the rubric of violence on women, that have led to robust campaigns against them by Saheli, along with other autonomous groups as well as Left party affiliated organisations such as All Indian Democratic Women's Association (AIDWA) and the National Federation of Indian Women (NFIW). Since the early 1980s, we mounted a firm resistance to the introduction of hazardous contraceptives, the lack of information, and sheer misinformation, campaigns surrounding them as well as unethical trials by State institutions such as the Indian Council for Medical Research (ICMR) that ironically, sets the ethical standards for trials on human subjects, while itself flagrantly violating them! And our strategies to do so were multifarious: in addition to leaflets, posters, plays and dharnas, when Hyderabad-based Stree Shakti Sanghatna discovered that women at a health camp were being deceived into participating in trials of Net-En, we were part of the protests that spread all over the country and culminated with us taking the ICMR and the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare to court in 1986. When Norplant was sought to be introduced through trials on about eighty thousand women we built a huge public resistance by demystifying its 'science' in the public domain, even creating a street play on the politics of population control, raising the issue with other women's groups and democratic rights groups to build a stronger support base for the campaign. At the international level too, we demanded that our feminist sisters make a paradigm shift to place what was happening to women's health in developing nations within global politics of population control, corporate and State interests in controlling women's fertility.

image.credit: Anti-Depo Provera protest. Photo Courtesy: Sama

content.en: For instance, in the early years of globalisation, Saheli along with many other Delhi-based women's groups, mounted a historic resistance to the introduction of Depo-Provera in India by taking over a press conference organised by the Max Pharma and its public relations agency, Mudra Diversified. The coordinated protest (along with its precursor in Mumbai) broke headlines all over the country and had a deterrent impact on the promotion/prescription of Depo Provera for many years. But today, with Depo Provera being approved for introduction into the Family Planning Programme, this anecdote gets relegated to the annals of nostalgia and history of the women's health movement. But in fact, it stands as a reminder of how complex battles against hazardous contraceptives have become in the post liberalisation 'free market', especially with widespread corporatisation of the media, where fewer and fewer stories of State or corporation (ir)responsibility find any place. The truth is that when even the most hazardous contraceptives and vaccines are marketed as 'free choice', we are hard-pressed to find a language that helps women see past these euphemisms, and find ways to safeguard their health, understand their sexuality, control their fertility and other life choices.

Since 1981, when Saheli was formally registered, we have waxed and waned in numbers but our organisational structure has remained that of a collective. We make decisions by consensus, have no formal hierarchy, and our only concession to leadership is the unenviable rotational job of being a monthly coordinator. Also related to this is the idea of the collective as the choice to challenge patriarchal and institutional hierarchies, the idea that notions like equality and care need to be reflected not just in our political goals but in the means to those goals, thus requiring us to consistently interrogate the structures of power and inequality that exist between us as a part of our larger feminist struggle.

As a small collective, Saheli understands that its greater strength lies in its collective action with others. So we join hands with like-minded groups and individuals on a range of campaigns: struggling with student groups to Reclaim the Night or for a Safe Campus in Delhi University; being part of platforms like the Dilli Janwaadi Adhikaar Manch on factory closures and workers' rights; working with democratic rights groups and anti-nuclear platforms against war, nuclear energy and militarisation in the north east. (One of the most long-standing feminist voices against militarised responses of the State to political conflict, Saheli has been central to struggles against draconian laws like the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act (AFSPA), the Unlawful Activities Prevention Act (UAPA), or even the gross misuse of the Indian Penal Code in states like Chhattisgarh.) We have a long history of working on wider platforms for peace and democracy. In solidarity with the struggles of activists like Irom Sharmila. In the face of communal conflicts - Delhi 1984 and 1992/3, Gujarat 2002, and Muzaffarnagar 2013. In the last few years, as part of the Women against Sexual Violence and State Repression (WSS) network we have worked on the widespread sexual violence on Dalit women and girls in Haryana. In the case of custodial torture of Adivasi activist Soni Sori or the hounding out of human rights lawyers from Chhattisgarh, together we have employed a mix of strategies - the power of street action, going to the courts, conducting fact findings, flooding the social media with information, mobilising national and international press - especially because the State in Chhattisgarh has no place for dissent, and the local press is either biased, scared or simply inflammatory against activists and human rights defenders. (As we write this, the Chhattisgarh Special Public Security Act has been invoked on seven human rights activists from Telangana on a fact-finding visit to Sukhma!). But every once in a while, when faced with the absolute refusal of the State to act in the course of justice, we are compelled to push ourselves to think of more creative ways to generate public awareness of the atrocities of the State. When the rape and murder of two young women allegedly by the Indian army in Shopian shook Jammu and Kashmir in 2009, and fact-finding missions, repeatedly implicated State agencies in the cover up to protect defence personnel, WSS launched the CBI: Cover-Up Bureau of India Campaign. A tongue in cheek mobilisation that resulted in us 'gifting' the CBI hundreds of bed-sheets with slogans against its dubious role in the Shopian investigation!

As activists, the dissemination of our ideas, politics and perspectives has always been a challenge. So at Saheli, women's 'study' and 'activism' have never been binary opposites. From the start, our activism has been sustained by research, feminist analysis, writing and dissemination. And so it is, Saheli is one of the very few autonomous women's groups with a long history of publishing: a (reasonably regular) newsletter in English and Hindi; fact finding reports, research reports, plays, leaflets, posters, booklets, the works. In the area of women's health for instance, we published a series of monographs on contraceptive and sterilisation methods, challenging their claims to safety and efficacy, and even guidebook on reproductive knowledge for young women (our very own Red Book), long before the language of 'sexuality' and 'choice' came to us. Then, there have been research studies and a play on sexual harassment at the workplace, and periodic publications that recap, review and reflect on Saheli's work over the years. In recent years, we have also been archiving older debates, creating online access to reports, newsletters, leaflets, posters and other published materials created over the decades. (Check out www.saheliwomen.org, or reach out to us at saheliwomen@gmail.com)

Take for instance, the study we undertook in the aftermath of the communal carnage of Muslims in Gujarat. Shaken by the widespread participation of women in the violence, we felt the need to understand how women are socialised into ideas of belonging to family and community (religious or otherwise), and how, their role as carriers of culture can feed into the kind of religious polarisation that we witnessed in 2002. This, despite the fact that it is women who bear the brunt of most cultural norms and mores! Around the same period, Saheli had also been engaging with issues and interlinkages between caste and gender, the power of patriarchy in maintaining caste hierarchies. (As a matter of fact, we later coordinated the Session on Women & Caste at the National Conference of Autonomous Women's Movements in Kolkata in 2006 with CADAM and Sama.) So we embarked on a study of how patriarchal institutions like marriage and family control women's sexuality, and explored its intersections with caste, community, class and religious identities. We spoke to women both within and outside the institution of marriage, women who had entered it through 'love' or family based arrangements, had crossed caste and community borders in doing so, or those who had stayed/become single, as well as some who were completely outside its ambit, like lesbian women. The results of this complex study were then published in 2007 as a report titled,
Talking Marriage, Caste and Community: Voices from Within.

While the report holds its own even today, we soon faced the question of how to take such complex discussions out into the public domain, in ways beyond the classical 'presentation' or 'talk'. We wanted to generate discussions and debates that would encourage reflections on women's relationships with families, communities, and cultures. And at the same time, create awareness of how these factors determine our constructions of 'otherness'. This dilemma then led to us to where Sahelis often end up: the creation of a new play called Kaun Jaat that sought to question categories of 'aurat jaat/mard jaat', 'unchi jaat/ neechi jaat', 'apni jaat/doosri jaat', and so on. A play in 5 monologues, Kaun Jaat featured a young woman Sapna in an arranged marriage, Rashmi/Reshma in an interreligious love marriage; Meenakshi, a Dalit doctor in a premium medical institute; Leena, a lesbian woman in an inter-caste relationship; and Bilkis/Manorama/Surekha/Sister M: a victim of communal/State violence who was sexually assaulted and/or killed because of their identity. All, not surprisingly, from marginalised communities - Dalit, Muslim, Christian and Tribal from the North East. All, attacked because of their gender, caste and community. All, made vulnerable by the deep-rooted patriarchal Brahmanism that creates and dominates the idea of the nation. As the satirical chorus of a song in the play set to a popular Hindi film track goes:

content: Yahan kiski kya kadr hai, meri jaan sabko khabar hai
Bach na saka koi, aye kitne
Khatra na le yaar, jaat samajh le
Hey, khatra na le yaar, jaat samajh le...
Everybody knows, how everyone is treated
No-one can escape the long hands of tra-di-tion...
So don't risk it, know your caste
Hey, don't risk it; know your caste...
Because everybody knows, who dominates whom...

content.en: Over time, the play (and its excerpted monologues) has become a powerful tool to generate discussions on these complex intersectionalities in colleges, at seminars, and even among comrade groups working to widen the ambit of 'the right to choice' beyond inter-caste and inter-religious alliances to same sex relationships. After all, we learn from each others' struggles and each others' trajectories of growth.

Thirty-five years on, Saheli is still in 'act'ivist mode, despite a slowing down of autonomous energies and politics across the nation. A challenge that has multiplied many fold with the State and street crackdown on all voices of dissent, attacks on secularists, people's movements, NGOs, students and marginalised communities, most often under the guise of the 'national good' and 'national security'. These are paradigms we need to challenge together today. We must strengthen our work with other movements to build resistance against the violations and excesses of the State, corporations and other vested powers in society, especially casteist and fundamentalist assertions of the right wing in every aspect of life. Only then can we hope to come closer to the idea of creating an egalitarian society where everyone can live with courage, justice and hope. Together.
